paragraphs.heading: A protein shell
paragraphs.text: A capsid is the shell of protein around a virus's genetic material. It is built from repeating protein units called protomers. The units you can actually make out in its 3-D shape are called capsomeres, and they may or may not match single proteins. The proteins themselves are called capsid proteins, or viral coat proteins.

paragraphs.heading: Core and envelope
paragraphs.text: The genome inside the capsid, sometimes with a core protein, is called the virus core, and capsid plus core together make the nucleocapsid. In enveloped viruses the capsid is coated with a lipid membrane, the viral envelope. The capsid gets this envelope from one of the host cell's membranes, such as the inner nuclear membrane, the Golgi membrane or the cell's outer membrane.

paragraphs.heading: Two common shapes
paragraphs.text: Most capsids are either helical or icosahedral. An icosahedron has 20 equal triangular faces and comes close to a sphere, while a helical capsid is shaped like a spring that fills the space of a cylinder without being one. Many rod-shaped and threadlike plant viruses are helical, and the best understood is the tobacco mosaic virus. Each of its coat proteins binds three nucleotides of its RNA, with 16.33 protein units per turn. Some viruses, such as bacteriophages, have more complicated shapes.

paragraphs.heading: Counting the pieces
paragraphs.text: An icosahedral capsid is made of 12 pentamers plus 10(T − 1) hexamers, where the T-number reflects how large and complex the capsid is. Each face can be made of one protein or of several; the foot-and-mouth disease virus uses three, named VP1–3. The heads of bacteriophages are often elongated icosahedra: a cylinder with a cap at each end.

paragraphs.heading: Building a capsid
paragraphs.text: After a virus infects a cell and starts copying itself, the cell's own protein-making machinery builds new capsid pieces. In some viruses, including helical ones and especially those with RNA genomes, the capsid proteins assemble together with the genome. In others, especially complex viruses with double-stranded DNA, the proteins first build an empty procapsid with a special portal at one corner. The viral DNA is then moved into the capsid through that portal.

paragraphs.heading: Protecting and delivering
paragraphs.text: The shell has to be stable enough to guard the genome against harm, such as extremes of pH or temperature and enzymes that break down proteins and nucleic acids. In viruses without an envelope, the capsid itself may take part in contact with receptors on the host cell, which leads to it crossing the cell membrane and getting inside. The genome is then released either by the capsid coming apart in the cytoplasm or by being pushed through a portal straight into the nucleus.

paragraphs.heading: Family trees from shells
paragraphs.text: The structure of the major capsid protein has been used to sort viruses into lineages. Bacteriophage PRD1, the algal virus PBCV-1, mimivirus and mammalian adenovirus share one lineage. Tailed double-stranded DNA bacteriophages and herpesviruses belong to another.
